Research complete. Note upfront: this session's WebSearch budget was exhausted before I started, so all verification was done via WebFetch (direct site fetches + DuckDuckGo HTML/Lite as a search proxy). Two key sites (pocket-concierge.jp, omakase.in) returned HTTP 403 to the fetcher, so those are verified indirectly only. Flagged throughout.

---

# 1. WHICH TIER GENUINELY NEEDS A RESERVATION

The honest cutoff is roughly **¥8,000–10,000 per person for dinner**. Below that, you can essentially always walk in (sometimes after a queue). Above it, assume you need a booking.

| Tier | Typical price (JPY, pp) | Reservation reality |
|---|---|---|
| Michelin 2–3★ / top-tier Tokyo sushi | ¥40,000–100,000+ dinner | Essential; many are effectively closed to newcomers (see §3) |
| High-end omakase sushi | ¥30,000–50,000 | Essential. 1–3 months out, often on a fixed release day |
| Mid-tier omakase sushi | ¥15,000–30,000 | Strongly recommended, but genuinely bookable online 2–6 weeks out. **This is the sweet spot for your trip.** |
| Entry omakase / lunch omakase | ¥6,000–12,000 | Book a few days ahead; lunch is far easier. TableCheck has many (e.g. Sushinosuke ¥8,800 course) |
| Kyoto kaiseki (ryotei, dinner) | ¥22,000–77,000 (Kikunoi Honten range, verified) | Essential; November is the hardest month (§4) |
| Kyoto kaiseki **lunch** | from ~¥9,900 | Book, but much easier — the single best value/access hack of the trip |
| Kobe/wagyu teppanyaki | course from ~¥11,000 (verified: Pontocho Noichi, Kyoto); Kobe-city venues run ¥15,000–30,000 dinner | Book 1–2 weeks ahead. Tourist-facing teppanyaki in Kyoto/Osaka is widely bookable via AutoReserve/Tabelog and takes walk-ins off-peak |
| Izakaya | ¥3,000–6,000 | Walk-in. Book only for groups 5+, or famous-name places on Fri/Sat |
| Ramen | ¥1,000–1,800 | Never bookable. Queue (§5) |
| Tonkatsu / tempura / donburi | ¥1,200–3,000 | Walk-in |
| Conveyor sushi (Sushiro, Kura, Hama) | ¥1,500–3,000 | Walk-in; use the in-store ticket kiosk or the chain's app to take a number remotely |
| Depachika (Isetan, Takashimaya, Daimaru) | ¥500–3,000 | No booking, ever. Best moderate-budget move in the whole country |

**Practical rule for two people, moderate budget:** book 2 splurges (one Tokyo mid-tier omakase, one Kyoto kaiseki lunch) and walk in for literally everything else.

---

# 2. HOW FOREIGNERS ACTUALLY BOOK

**TableCheck** — https://www.tablecheck.com/en/japan
Verified live and fully English. Japan-based reservation OS used by thousands of restaurants incl. most major hotel restaurants. Takes international cards; has TableCheck Pay. Deposit/cancellation is set per-restaurant (many mid-tier places take no card at all). Currently running "Tokyo/Kyoto Bishoku Meguri 2026 Summer" campaigns and a Visa 10%-off promo. **Best first stop for a moderate-budget traveler.**

**OMAKASE** — https://omakase.in/en (site 403'd my fetcher; details verified via secondary sources)
GMO-run, English-language, official Michelin Guide partner. Aimed at top sushi/fine dining. Slots release on a **fixed monthly schedule, typically the 1st**, and famous counters vanish in seconds. Charges a **¥390-per-seat reservation fee**; a paid premium tier (~¥3,000/month) gets earlier access. Cancellation terms set per-restaurant. Foreign cards accepted.

**Pocket Concierge** — https://pocket-concierge.jp (site 403'd; **status verified indirectly — it still appears to be operating in 2026**)
Amex-owned since Jan 2019. ~800 high-end restaurants, Tokyo/Yokohama/Kyoto/Osaka. English + Japanese concierge. **Prepaid** model — you pay at booking, which neatly solves the foreign-card and no-show-trust problem. Cancellation: 100% same-day, 50% within 2–3 business days. Especially useful for Amex Platinum/Centurion holders, who get access to some otherwise-unreachable seats. *Caveat: I could not load the site directly to confirm it is live today — verify before relying on it.*

**Tabelog English** — https://tabelog.com/en/
Japan's largest restaurant database (900,000+ listings) and the authoritative source for whether a place exists, its hours, and its real price band. **Booking is the weak point**: only a subset of listings are bookable in English, and travellers routinely report having to fall back on browser translation of the Japanese site to complete a reservation. Use it for research; use something else to book.

**Ikyu Restaurant** — https://restaurant.ikyu.com
Premium/kaiseki-heavy, and the best inventory for Kyoto ryotei. **Effectively Japanese-only** — reported as requiring browser translation. Supports online card payment with an authentication step (3D Secure), which is where foreign cards often fail. Some restaurants decline foreign bookings via Ikyu and redirect you elsewhere. Workable but frustrating.

**AutoReserve** — https://autoreserve.com
Newer app-based player, international-guest friendly, real-time booking, and notably it will place the phone call in Japanese on your behalf for restaurants that aren't online. Good coverage of mid-tier including Kyoto/Osaka teppanyaki.

**byFood** — https://www.byfood.com
Food-tour marketplace with a reservation-assistance arm explicitly aimed at restaurants "inaccessible to non-Japanese speakers." English throughout, foreign cards fine.

**Paid concierge / booking agents** (verified names and fees):
- TableAll — https://tableall.com — **$30–100 per booking**, positioned for "impossible reservations"
- BookNippon — https://booknippon.com — **from $15**, standard bookings refunded if they can't get you in. Best value.
- My Concierge Japan — https://myconciergejapan.com — multilingual, Michelin-focused, fee not published
- Japan Travel Concierge (Juno) — https://japantravelconcierge.com — **plans from $199**, full itinerary
- ToU Menu — https://toumenu.com/en/concierge and JapanFoodTravel — https://japanfood.travel — messaging-app based, fees not published

**Hotel concierge** — free, and still the single highest-success-rate route for anything hard. A 4–5★ Tokyo/Kyoto hotel concierge can call in Japanese, vouch for you, and supply the hotel's own phone number as the contact. Email them **at booking time**, not on arrival.

**Direct phone / Google Maps** — Google Maps "Reserve a table" is increasingly wired into TableCheck/AutoReserve inventory and is worth checking. Direct phone works only if someone speaks English or you have a Japanese speaker.

---

# 3. THE REALITY: PLACES YOU SIMPLY CANNOT GET INTO

Be honest with yourselves — a meaningful slice of Japan's best dining is closed to you, and no amount of money or planning fixes it.

**Ichigensan okotowari (一見さんお断り)** — "no first-time customers." Concentrated in Kyoto (Gion ryotei, ochaya) but present in Tokyo too. Originates in the historical *kake* running-tab credit system, not xenophobia: the house extended credit, so it needed a guarantor. Today it functions as a trust and atmosphere filter. The only key is an introduction from an existing patron — a hotel concierge at a top-tier ryokan/hotel can sometimes act as that guarantor, which is exactly why the concierge route matters more in Kyoto than anywhere else.

**Introduction-only sushi.** Verified example: **Sushi Saito** (Roppongi, 8 counter seats) — described as impossible to book without being a regular or having a personal introduction; even with one, 3–6 months. Sushi Sugita sits in the same category. Treat these as off the table and stop spending energy on them.

**Japanese-phone-number walls.** Many booking forms hard-require a domestic mobile number. Workarounds, in order of effectiveness: (1) use your hotel's phone number and name, (2) book on a platform that doesn't ask (TableCheck, OMAKASE, Pocket Concierge), (3) get a Japanese SIM/eSIM with a real number, (4) use a paid agent whose number goes on the booking.

**Foreign-card / 3D Secure failures.** High-end places hold a card against no-shows, and 3D Secure 2.0 authentication frequently fails with non-Japanese issuers. Mitigations: use a prepaid platform (Pocket Concierge), notify your bank of travel, have a second card from a different network ready, and prefer Amex if you have it.

**No-show deposit culture.** Verified typical high-end terms: **100% of the meal price same-day, 50% within 2–3 business days**, with per-person exposure of **¥30,000–50,000**. This is real and enforced. Do not speculatively book multiple high-end restaurants for the same night.

**The honest bottom line:** with a moderate budget and no connections, roughly the top 1–2% of Japanese restaurants are inaccessible. The consolation is genuine — the ¥15,000–30,000 mid-tier omakase band and the ¥9,900–15,000 kaiseki lunch band are excellent, bookable, and where most of the actual pleasure lives.

---

# 4. HOW FAR AHEAD — AND WHAT NOVEMBER 2026 MEANS

You are travelling in **the single hardest month in Kyoto**. Peak foliage 2026 is roughly **Nov 20 – early Dec**; Kyoto hotel rates rise 50–100% and sell out across all categories.

| Target | Book by |
|---|---|
| Top-tier / Michelin-starred | **2–3 months ahead**, on the release day |
| Popular sushi counters | **~1 month ahead** |
| OMAKASE-listed sushi | The **1st of the month**, at the release hour, ready to click. Slots go in seconds. |
| Kyoto ryotei kaiseki, November dinner | **2–3 months ahead** — i.e. book in **August/September 2026** |
| Kyoto kaiseki lunch | 3–4 weeks |
| Mid-tier omakase, teppanyaki | 2–4 weeks |
| Izakaya, groups | 2–5 days |

**Since it is now August 2026, you are almost exactly on time for the hardest bookings — this is the month to act on Kyoto kaiseki dinner and any starred Tokyo restaurant.**

**What actually happens at 2 weeks out (late October):** Tokyo mid-tier omakase — fine, especially weekday and lunch. Kyoto kaiseki dinner on a foliage weekend — realistically nothing at the famous houses; you'll be looking at lunch slots, weekday-only availability, hotel restaurants, or Osaka instead. Michelin-starred anything — no. Cancellations do surface, so set alerts on TableCheck/OMAKASE and have a concierge watching, but do not build the trip around it.

---

# 5. WALK-IN PLACES WORTH THE QUEUE

**Tokyo — ramen** (never bookable; all cash-or-ticket-machine)
- **Fuunji**, Shinjuku — tsukemen, ~¥1,200. Queue "tens of minutes, not hours." Go at 11:00 or after 20:00.
- **Tsuta**, Yoyogi-Uehara — world's first Michelin-starred ramen, truffle shoyu, ~¥1,500–1,800. **Verified: since relocating from Sugamo it no longer uses the advance ticket system** — just queue.
- **Nakiryu**, Otsuka — tantanmen **¥1,200**. **Verified: since 2024 a tablet at the entrance issues numbered entry tickets from 08:00** on operating days, so no dawn queuing. Closed Sundays/holidays. Bib Gourmand (was starred).
- **Ichiran** — **¥1,080** (2026), 24h at some branches with a 22:00–06:00 late-night surcharge. Solo booths, order sheet, walk-in only, no app queue. Two Shibuya locations.
- **Ramen Jiro** — ~¥800–1,000, huge portions, 30–60 min queues, strict unwritten etiquette. Fun but not a beginner's stop.
- **Rokurinsha**, Tokyo Station Ramen Street — tsukemen, ~¥1,200, reliably 30–60 min.

## Japan transport plan — 10 days, 2 people, November 2026
Route: NRT/HND → Tokyo → Hakone → Kyoto (+ Nara day trip) → Osaka → KIX. **All figures per person, one-way, adult, unless noted.**

### ⚠️ Two things that changed recently — check these first
- **JR East raised fares on 14 March 2026** (avg +7.1%, first real rise since 1987). Yamanote minimum went ¥150 → **¥160**; the discount "Yamanote-area" fare band was abolished. Any guide written before March 2026 understates Tokyo JR fares. ([JR East revision](https://www.jreast.co.jp/en/2026unchin-kaitei/), [Time Out](https://www.timeout.com/tokyo/news/jr-east-is-raising-its-prices-starting-in-march-2026-080425))
- **JR Pass 7-day ordinary is ¥50,000** (unchanged), but **from 1 Oct 2026 overseas travel-agency sales rise to ¥53,000**; buying direct on the official JR site stays ¥50,000. ([japan-guide, upd. 1 Apr 2026](https://www.japan-guide.com/e/e2361.html))

---

## 1. Airport transfers

**Narita → central Tokyo**
| Option | Fare | Time |
|---|---|---|
| N'EX to Tokyo Stn | **¥3,070** | 53–60 min |
| N'EX to Shinjuku/Shibuya/Ikebukuro | **¥3,250** | ~80–85 min |
| **N'EX TOKYO Round Trip Ticket** (foreign passport, 14 days) | **¥5,200** | — |
| Keisei Skyliner → Nippori/Ueno | **¥2,470** (¥2,465 IC) | 41–43 min |
| Skyliner advance/online | ~¥2,310 | — |
| Keisei Main Line ltd exp (no surcharge) | ~¥1,260 | 90–100 min |
| **Airport Bus TYO-NRT** → Tokyo Stn/Ginza | **¥1,500** (¥3,000 late-night) | 65–90 min |
| Airport Limousine | ~¥3,100 | ~100 min |

⚠️ **Flag:** the N'EX ¥3,070 is contested — one 2026 source says it's pre-March-revision, another says post. The round-trip ticket demonstrably rose ¥5,000 → ¥5,200 on 14 Mar 2026, so **assume ~¥3,070–3,300**. Skyliner ¥2,470 is from Keisei's own fare page and is solid.

**Haneda → central Tokyo**
| Option | Fare | Time |
|---|---|---|
| Tokyo Monorail → Hamamatsucho | **¥520** (¥519 IC) | 13–18 min |
| Monorail + Yamanote to Tokyo Stn | ~¥700 total | 20–30 min |
| **Keikyu → Shinagawa** | **¥327 IC** | 11–14 min |
| Keikyu through-service → Higashi-Ginza/Asakusa | ¥599 IC | ~32 min |
| Keikyu + JR → Shinjuku | ¥535 IC | 30–35 min |
| Limousine bus → Shinjuku / Tokyo Stn | ¥1,400 / ¥1,200 | 45–60 min |
| Taxi flat fare → Tokyo Stn | ¥7,600 (¥9,000 late) | 20–40 min |

**Haneda is dramatically cheaper than Narita** — if you have a choice of arrival airport, that's worth ~¥2,700/person.

**Kyoto / Osaka → KIX**
| Option | Fare | Time |
|---|---|---|
| Nankai **Rapi:t** → Namba | ¥1,490 | ~35 min |
| Nankai **Airport Express** → Namba | ¥970 | ~45 min |
| JR Airport Rapid → Namba (via Tennoji) | ¥1,060 | ~60 min |
| Limousine bus → OCAT/Namba | ¥1,300 | ~50 min |
| JR **Haruka** → Tennoji / Shin-Osaka / **Kyoto** | ¥1,300 / ¥1,800 / **¥2,200** | 46 / 50 / **73–75 min** |

⚠️ **Flag (important):** the Nankai/bus figures are from a japan-guide page last updated **April 2024** and Nankai has revised fares since — treat as ±10%. The Haruka figures are from a source dated Apr 2025 and **look like the discounted tourist fares, not the full walk-up fare** (full Kyoto–KIX Haruka reserved is materially higher). I could not confirm the current ICOCA & HARUKA package price from a live source. **Verify Haruka and Nankai before budgeting tightly.**

---

## 2. Nationwide JR Pass: **NO — don't buy it.** Here's the arithmetic.

Sum of every **JR-eligible** leg on this exact itinerary:

| Leg | Cost |
|---|---|
| Narita → Tokyo (N'EX) | ¥3,070 |
| Tokyo → Odawara (Hikari/Kodama, non-reserved) | ¥3,370 |
| Odawara → Kyoto (Hikari, non-reserved) | ¥11,770 |
| Kyoto ⇄ Nara (JR Nara Line, return) | ¥1,440 |
| Kyoto → Osaka (JR) | ¥580 |
| Osaka → KIX (JR Airport Rapid) | ¥1,060 |
| **Total JR-eligible** | **≈ ¥21,290** |

**7-day JR Pass: ¥50,000. You would lose ≈ ¥28,700 per person (¥57,400 for two).**

Three further reasons it fails here:
1. **It's 7 days against a 10-day trip** — the two airport transfers sit at opposite ends and can't both be inside the window.
2. **Hakone is almost entirely non-JR** (Odakyu, Tozan, ropeway, cruise) — the pass covers none of it.
3. **Nozomi/Mizuho now require a supplement even with the pass** — ¥4,960 Tokyo→Kyoto. ([japan-guide](https://www.japan-guide.com/e/e2361.html))

The pass only breaks even around a Tokyo–Kyoto–Hiroshima–Tokyo pattern. You aren't doing that.

**Regional alternatives — verdict on each:**

| Pass | Price | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **Hakone Free Pass 2-day (Shinjuku)** | **¥7,100** | ✅ **Buy.** Clear win — see §4. |
| **JR Kansai Area Pass 1-day** | **¥2,800** | 🟡 Marginal. Covers Haruka *reserved* to KIX (up to 2 reservations) plus Kyoto–Osaka–Nara–Kobe JR. Worth it **only** if you use it on a day combining Nara + the airport run, or if the walk-up Haruka fare exceeds ¥2,800. ([JR West](http://www.westjr.co.jp/travel-information/en/tickets-passes/jrwest-rail-pass/kansai/)) |
| **JR Kansai Area Pass 2/3/4-day** | ¥4,800 / ¥5,800 / ¥7,000 | ❌ Your Kansai JR legs total ~¥3,000. Won't pay off. |
| **Kansai Thru Pass** | ⚠️ **unconfirmed** | Covers non-JR (subways, Hankyu/Keihan/Kintetsu/Nankai) incl. Nankai to KIX. Plausibly worth it on a Kyoto+Osaka+Nara combo — **verify current price.** |
| **JR Tokyo Wide Pass** | ⚠️ **unconfirmed price** | ❌ Regardless: it covers Odawara but **not** Hakone Tozan/ropeway/cruise, and your only qualifying leg is a ¥3,370 hop. Only pays off if you add Nikko/Karuizawa/Gala. |

**Recommendation: point-to-point tickets + the Hakone Free Pass.** Buy shinkansen tickets at the machine or via smartEX; no pass math needed.

---

## 3. Point-to-point shinkansen

Fare = **base fare + limited-express charge**. Tokyo→Kyoto is base ¥8,360 + LEX charge.

| Leg | Non-reserved | Reserved | Time |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tokyo → Odawara (Hikari/Kodama) | ¥3,370 | ¥4,270 | ~27 min (Hikari), 35–40 (Kodama) |
| **Odawara → Kyoto** (Hikari) | **¥11,770** | **¥12,300** | 1h43–2h05 (Kodama ~2h50) |
| Tokyo → Kyoto direct — Hikari | ¥13,320 | ¥13,850 | ~2h40 |
| Tokyo → Kyoto direct — **Nozomi** | — | **¥14,170** | 2h13 |
| Kyoto → Shin-Osaka (Hikari/Kodama) | ¥1,450 | ¥2,870 | 12–15 min |
| Kyoto → Osaka (conventional JR, no shinkansen) | ¥580 | — | ~29 min |
| Kyoto → Nara (JR Miyakoji Rapid) | ¥720 | — | 45 min |
| Kyoto → Nara (Kintetsu ltd exp / regular) | ¥1,280 / ¥760 | — | 35 / 45 min |

Notes:
- **Nozomi does not stop at Odawara.** Hakone traffic must use Hikari or Kodama.
- **Reserved costs ¥530 more than non-reserved** on the Tokyo–Kyoto stretch. The ~¥320 gap between Nozomi and Hikari reserved is the Nozomi premium.
- **Nozomi still has 2 non-reserved cars** in normal periods, going fully-reserved only over long weekends, New Year, Golden Week and Obon. ([japan-guide, upd. 9 May 2026](https://www.japan-guide.com/e/e2018_tokaido.html)) — I saw a widely-repeated blog claim that Nozomi went all-reserved in March 2024; **that appears to be wrong.**
- **With a JR Pass**, Nozomi/Mizuho need a supplement (¥4,960 Tokyo–Kyoto); Hikari/Kodama/Sakura are free.
- ⚠️ Reserved-seat charges flex by season (roughly −¥200 off-peak / +¥200 peak / +¥400 super-peak; Tokyo–Kyoto reserved ranges ¥13,650–¥14,250). **I could not confirm November's classification** — most of November is regular season with scattered off-peak weekdays, but verify at booking.
- **Skipping Hakone doesn't save money:** Tokyo→Odawara + Odawara→Kyoto = ¥15,140 non-reserved vs ¥13,320 direct. Hakone costs you ~¥1,800 in extra rail, which is the price of the stopover.

---

## 4. Hakone — buy the Free Pass

Straight from Odakyu's official site ([odakyu-global.com](https://odakyu-global.com/passes/hakone-freepass/)):

| Pass | Adult | Child |
|---|---|---|
| **2-day from Shinjuku** | **¥7,100** | ¥1,600 |
| 3-day from Shinjuku | ¥7,500 | ¥1,850 |
| **2-day from Odawara** (Hakone area only) | **¥6,000** | ¥1,500 |
| 3-day from Odawara | ¥6,400 | ¥1,750 |

**Covers 8 modes, unlimited:** Odakyu Line (Shinjuku↔Odawara round trip on the Shinjuku version), Hakone Tozan Train, Hakone Tozan Cable Car, Hakone Ropeway, Hakone Sightseeing Cruise (the pirate ship), Hakone Tozan Bus in designated areas, the "Kanko Shisetsu-Meguri" tourist bus, and Odakyu Highway Bus / Tokai Bus in designated areas.

**Does NOT cover:** the **Romancecar limited-express surcharge — ¥1,200 adult / ¥600 child** Shinjuku→Hakone-Yumoto, bought separately on top of the pass. Without it you ride regular express trains free on the pass (slower, one transfer at Odawara).

**Buy it:** EMot Online Tickets app (fully digital), Odakyu Sightseeing Service Centers, or ticket vending machines. Available at Odawara.

**Is it worth it?** Yes, and it isn't close. The standard loop — Tozan train, cable car, ropeway, pirate ship, bus back — runs roughly ¥5,000–6,000 in individual fares from Odawara *before* you add Shinjuku↔Odawara (~¥900 each way). The ¥7,100 Shinjuku 2-day beats paying à la carte on essentially any itinerary that completes the loop.

**Shinjuku vs Odawara version for your route:** since you leave Hakone eastward-to-Kyoto rather than returning to Shinjuku, you're not using the Shinjuku pass's return leg. Odawara 2-day (¥6,000) + a one-way Odakyu Shinjuku→Odawara (~¥900) ≈ ¥6,900 — a wash against ¥7,100. **Take the Shinjuku version for simplicity**, or the Odawara version if you're already at Odawara.

---

## 5. Luggage — forward it, and here's why it's not optional

**Shinkansen oversized baggage rule (still in force 2026)** — [JR Central official](https://global.jr-central.co.jp/en/info/oversized-baggage/):
- Baggage with **3 dimensions summing 160–250 cm requires a free advance "oversized baggage area" seat reservation.**
- **Over 250 cm: banned outright.**
- The reservation **costs nothing extra** (same price as a normal reserved seat) — you get the last row of the car with the space behind it.
- **Boarding without one: ¥1,000 penalty**, and staff stow the bag wherever they can.
- **Non-reserved cars have no oversized baggage areas** — you may not bring a 160cm+ bag into non-reserved seating at all.

**This is the catch:** a typical large check-in suitcase is ~155–165 cm total, right on the line. The cheap non-reserved Odawara→Kyoto ticket (¥11,770) is exactly what you *can't* use with a big suitcase.

**Yamato TA-Q-BIN, Tokyo → Kyoto, one bag** (official table, rates effective 1 Oct 2025):

| Size | Fare |
|---|---|
| 100 | ¥1,650 |
| **120** | **¥2,170** |
| **140** | **¥2,780** |
| **160** | **¥3,160** |

**Budget ¥2,200–3,200 per bag.** Next-day delivery is standard on this corridor (allow 1–2 days). Drop at your hotel front desk (usual tourist route, normally free), or a konbini for a **−¥100 discount**, or a Yamato office for **−¥100/−¥150**. Max 200 cm / 30 kg. ⚠️ Confirm your Kyoto lodging accepts deliveries — unmanned/Airbnb-type places often can't.

**Airport forwarding:** Narita/Haneda → Tokyo hotel ~¥1,600–3,680 by size (Haneda same-day ¥4,610; Narita same-day cutoffs 10:30 T1/T2, 09:50 T3). ⚠️ Kyoto/Osaka hotel → KIX pricing I could only confirm indirectly (~¥3,700 range) — verify with your hotel.

**Verdict: forward one bag each Tokyo→Kyoto for ~¥2,600.** It costs about the same as the reserved-seat upgrade you'd otherwise be forced into, and you travel Tokyo→Hakone→Kyoto with a daypack instead of hauling suitcases through the Hakone loop's six transfers. This is the single best-value ¥2,600 on the trip.

## 6. IC cards & local transport

**The card shortage is over.** Unregistered Suica and PASMO returned to sale **1 March 2025** and are freely available from station machines in 2026 (¥500 refundable deposit, ¥220 refund fee). ([Time Out](https://www.timeout.com/tokyo/news/unregistered-suica-and-pasmo-transport-cards-to-resume-sales-from-march-022125))

| Option | Deal |
|---|---|
| Regular Suica/PASMO/ICOCA | ¥500 deposit + charge; 10-yr validity |
| **Welcome Suica** (physical) | No deposit, **28 days**, balance non-refundable; Haneda/Narita + major JR stations |
| **Welcome Suica Mobile** | Free, no deposit, **180 days**, **iPhone only** (launched Mar 2025) |
| Mobile Suica in Apple Wallet | ✅ Works with a **non-Japanese Apple ID**. **Top-up: Mastercard/Amex/JCB work; foreign-issued Visa is blocked.** Cash top-up at any machine always works. |
| Android | ❌ **Effectively unavailable** — needs Osaifu-Keitai hardware absent on non-Japan phones |
| **TOURIST PASMO** | PASMO Passport was discontinued Oct 2024; successor launched **20 May 2026** — no deposit, 28 days, Haneda/Narita only |

|---|---|---|
| 2023 | **Nov 26** | **Dec 4** |
| 2024 | **Nov 28** (still peak Dec 4) | **Dec 3** |
| 2025 | **~Nov 22** (report Nov 29 said peak "started about a week ago") | **Nov 26** |

Sources: [koyo23](https://www.japan-guide.com/blog/koyo23/), [koyo24](https://www.japan-guide.com/blog/koyo24/), [koyo25](https://www.japan-guide.com/blog/koyo25/), [Kyoto 11/29/25](https://www.japan-guide.com/blog/koyo25/251129_kyoto.html), [Tokyo 12/2/25](https://www.japan-guide.com/blog/koyo25/251202_tokyo.html).

**Nuance worth knowing:** japan-guide's [Tokyo 26 Nov 2025 report](https://www.japan-guide.com/blog/koyo25/251126_tokyo.html) explicitly said the 2025 peak "aligns quite closely with the typical year," crediting below-average autumn temperatures. So it is not a clean monotonic drift later — 2023 and 2024 were late, 2025 was roughly normal. The mechanism is warm autumn nights delaying color, so it varies year to year.

For 2026 the early signal points late again: the JMA forecast above-normal summer temperatures nationwide, and secondary forecasters are projecting **3–5 days later than historical average**, with Kyoto/Osaka landing in the final week of November or early December. Treat that as a projection until the September forecasts land.

**A second 2025 phenomenon to watch for:** japan-guide's Kyoto reports noted "a considerable number of maple trees whose leaves have prematurely dried up," attributed to above-average summer heat and below-average rainfall. If the 2026 summer is similarly hot and dry, expect patchy quality even at peak.

### Tokyo — typical windows

Per [japan-guide's Tokyo spots page](https://www.japan-guide.com/e/e3061.html):

| Spot | Typical best |
|---|---|
| **Rikugien** | Late Nov – early Dec |
| **Koishikawa Korakuen** | Late Nov – early Dec |
| **Meiji Jingu Gaien Icho Namiki (ginkgo)** | Late Nov – early Dec |
| **Showa Memorial (Kinen) Park** | **Late Oct – late Nov** (earliest of the group) |
| Shinjuku Gyoen | Mid Nov – mid Dec |
| Mount Takao | Mid – late Nov |
| Yoyogi Park / Imperial East Garden / Hama Rikyu | Late Nov – early Dec |

GO TOKYO's official line: **"mid-November to early December"** overall, with a specific warning that "weekends and holidays are particularly crowded" — go weekday mornings ([gotokyo.org](https://www.gotokyo.org/en/story/guide/autumn-leaves-forecast/index.html)).

Practical note on the ginkgo: **ginkgo runs ~1 week ahead of maple.** In 2025 the Gaien Icho Namiki was "spectacular for several days already" by Nov 26 with center-street trees already dropping leaves, while Rikugien/Koishikawa maples didn't hit best until early December. **You generally cannot catch peak ginkgo and peak maple in Tokyo on the same day** — if the trip is short, pick one. Showa Kinen Park (admission ¥450, [japan-guide](https://www.japan-guide.com/e/e3034.html)) is ginkgo-led and therefore earlier — it's the best bet for early-to-mid November.

### Hakone — this is an elevation gradient, not a date

Hakone spans ~110 m at Hakone-Yumoto to ~1,000 m at Owakudani and ~1,400 m at the peaks, which spreads the season over 4+ weeks. japan-guide gives the region a blanket "early to late November" ([where-to-see page](https://www.japan-guide.com/e/e2014_where.html)); the finer breakdown:

| Area | Approx. elevation | Typical peak |
|---|---|---|
| Mt. Kamiyama / Mt. Kintoki peaks | 1,200–1,400 m | Late October |
| **Owakudani** (ropeway) | ~1,000 m | **Late Oct – mid Nov** |
| **Sengokuhara** (also the pampas grass) | ~645 m | **Early–mid Nov** |
| **Lake Ashi / Moto-Hakone** | ~725 m | **Early–mid Nov** |
| Gora / Miyanoshita | ~550/430 m | Mid–late Nov |
| **Hakone-Yumoto** | ~110 m | **Late Nov – early Dec** |

This is the single most useful planning fact in the whole brief: **Hakone is forgiving.** Whatever week in November you go, doing the standard loop (Yumoto → Tozan train → cablecar → ropeway/Owakudani → boat on Ashi → bus) crosses roughly 900 m of elevation in one day, so you will hit *something* at peak. Sengokuhara pampas grass holds well almost to the end of November.

Note Sengokuhara/Gora run **3–4 °C colder than Hakone-Yumoto** — dress for the top of the mountain, not the station.

### Kyoto — typical windows

Per [japan-guide's Kyoto spots page](https://www.japan-guide.com/e/e3953.html):

- **Mid November:** Takao (Jingoji), Ohara Sanzenin — the earliest, both are up in the hills
- **Mid–late November:** Tofukuji, Shinnyodo, Enkoji, Daigoji, Yoshiminedera, Shugakuin Imperial Villa
- **Late Nov – early Dec:** Arashiyama, Kiyomizudera, Eikando, Nanzenji, Kodaiji, Chionin, Shorenin
- Kitano Tenmangu: mid Nov – early Dec

Same elevation logic as Hakone in miniature — the northern hill sites (Takao, Ohara, Kurama) go ~1–2 weeks before the city-floor Higashiyama temples.

### Nara

Nara is treated as one timeline rather than site-by-site. Season runs roughly **15 Oct – 15 Dec with peak around 15 November** in an average year ([Inside Kyoto](https://www.insidekyoto.com/nara-fall-foliage)). Best areas: Nara Park generally, the walk up to Nigatsudo/Sangatsudo behind Todaiji, and the wooded paths around Kasuga Taisha. Given the recent late trend, plan for **late November** rather than mid.

### Bonus for the Osaka leg
**Minoo Park** (Minoo Falls) — "usually best in the second half of November," ~25 min and **¥280** from Umeda via Hankyu, then a 3 km / 45-min paved valley walk to the 33 m waterfall, free entry ([japan-guide](https://www.japan-guide.com/e/e4019.html)). The best foliage that's genuinely close to Osaka.

### Bottom line on timing
For a single trip covering Tokyo + Hakone + Kyoto + Nara, the sweet spot is roughly **Nov 18 – Dec 2**. Earlier than ~Nov 15 and Kyoto/Nara/Tokyo maples will be green; that window does, however, catch high-elevation Hakone and Showa Kinen ginkgo at their best. The trade-off is brutal: peak foliage weeks are also peak crowd weeks (§3).

## 2. Weather and packing

November averages (highs/lows, rainfall):

| City | Avg high | Avg low | Rainfall | Rainy days |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Tokyo** | 18 °C / 64 °F | 10 °C / 50 °F | 96 mm | ~13 |
| **Hakone** (town avg) | 17.5 °C | 7.1 °C | 139 mm | ~11 |
| **Kyoto** | 17 °C / 63 °F | 7 °C / 45 °F | 84 mm | ~16 |
| **Osaka** | 18 °C / 64 °F | 9 °C / 48 °F | 82 mm | ~14 |
| **Nara** | 16.5 °C | 6.4 °C | 71 mm | ~8 |

Sources: [Tokyo](https://weather-and-climate.com/Tokyo-November-averages), [Kyoto](https://weather-and-climate.com/kyoto-November-averages), [Osaka](https://weather-and-climate.com/osaka-November-averages), [Hakone](https://weather-and-climate.com/hakone-November-averages), [Nara](https://www.weather-atlas.com/en/japan/nara-weather-november). These are aggregator figures, broadly consistent with JMA 1991–2020 normals; I could not pull the JMA English normals table cleanly, so treat them as ±1 °C.

**Early vs late November is a real difference, not a rounding error.** Kyoto drops from ~20 °C at the start of the month to ~14 °C by the end; Nara from ~19 °C to ~14 °C. Early November is light-jacket weather; late November mornings and evenings are genuinely cold, especially inland Kyoto/Nara where the overnight low sits near 5 °C.

Three things that break naive packing:

1. **Diurnal swing, not absolute cold.** Kyoto's 17/7 °C spread means a 10 °C change within a day. Kyoto and Nara are basins — they trap cold air overnight and the mornings bite far more than "average high 17 °C" suggests.
2. **Hakone is a different climate zone.** The 17.5/7.1 °C figure is the town average; Sengokuhara and Gora run 3–4 °C colder, and Owakudani at ~1,000 m is colder again and windy on the ropeway. Bring a proper insulating layer for the Hakone day even if Tokyo is mild.
3. **Evening illuminations are the coldest thing you'll do.** Kyoto temple light-ups and the Gaien ginkgo light-up run to 19:30–21:00, standing still, in late November. This is where people are underdressed.

**Pack:** merino/synthetic base layers; a mid-layer fleece or light down (packable down is ideal — it handles Owakudani and stuffs into a daypack the rest of the time); a **water-resistant** shell rather than a wool coat (Kyoto averages ~16 rainy days in November — the wettest of the five by frequency, though the totals are modest, so it's drizzle rather than downpours); a compact umbrella (universally used in Japan, cheap at any konbini if you'd rather buy on arrival); **comfortable waterproof-ish walking shoes** — Kyoto/Nara temple days run 15–20 k steps on gravel and stone; and **easily removable shoes** since you'll be in and out of temples constantly — loafers or zip boots beat laces. Add a light scarf and gloves if you're travelling late November. Onsen ryokan supply yukata and towels, so don't pack sleepwear for Hakone.

## 3. Public holidays and crowding

**Confirmed against the Japanese Cabinet Office** ([cao.go.jp](https://www8.cao.go.jp/chosei/shukujitsu/gaiyou.html)) and [publicholidays.jp](https://publicholidays.jp/2026-dates/):

| Holiday | Date | Day |
|---|---|---|
| **Culture Day (文化の日)** | **3 November 2026** | **Tuesday** |
| **Labour Thanksgiving Day (勤労感謝の日)** | **23 November 2026** | **Monday** |

**No substitute holiday (振替休日) applies in November 2026.** Substitute holidays only trigger when a holiday falls on a Sunday; neither does. (2026 does have substitute/bridge days, but they fall on **6 May** and **22 September** — not November.)

November 2026 weekends: **Nov 7–8, 14–15, 21–22, 28–29.** Nov 1 is a Sunday.

### What this means in practice

- **Mon 2 Nov is a bridge day.** With Culture Day on a Tuesday, large numbers of Japanese workers take Monday 2 Nov off to make Sat 31 Oct – Tue 3 Nov a four-day break. **Treat Oct 31 – Nov 3 as a domestic travel peak.** Hakone, Nikko and Kyoto hotels will be expensive and full; book well ahead.
- **Sat 21 – Mon 23 Nov is a true three-day weekend** (Labour Thanksgiving on a Monday). This is the single worst period of the entire trip window, because **it collides almost exactly with peak Kyoto foliage.** If your dates are flexible at all, avoid Kyoto on 21–23 November. If they aren't, do Kyoto's marquee sites at dawn and save the three-day weekend for something lower-profile.
- **Sat 7 Nov** is a double-hit in Tokyo: Ichi-no-tori (§4) falls on a Saturday, which is unusual and drives much heavier crowds than a weekday fair.
- **Sun 15 Nov is Shichi-Go-San** — major congestion at Meiji Jingu, Hie Shrine, Tomioka Hachimangu and the surrounding weekends, plus lots of families in formal dress (charming, but slow-moving).
- **Tue 3 Nov (Culture Day)** in Hakone means the Daimyo Gyoretsu procession closes Route 1 through Hakone-Yumoto roughly 11:00–15:00. Do not plan to move around Hakone by car or bus that afternoon.

### Kyoto weekend crowding generally

The **last two weeks of November are among the most crowded periods in Kyoto's entire year**, and weekends within the Nov 18–30 window are severely congested at the headline sites. Specific mitigations that actually work:

- **Weekday mornings before 10:00.** On weekends and holidays, make it **08:00**.
- **Kiyomizudera opens at 06:00** — arriving at opening is the single highest-leverage move in Kyoto.
- **Tofukuji** is the worst offender: large crowds form immediately at opening, and the Tsutenkyo Bridge becomes a no-stopping shuffle. japan-guide's 21 Nov 2025 report flagged it explicitly. There is a reservation-only early-morning private viewing worth investigating.
- **Philosopher's Path after 16:00** is pleasant when the day-trippers have gone.
- Kyoto City is actively pushing six peripheral districts — **Fushimi, Ohara, Takao, Yamashina, Nishikyo, Keihoku** — to decompress the centre. Ohara and Takao also peak *earlier* (mid-Nov), so they solve a timing problem and a crowd problem at once.

## 5. Money: taxes, JR Pass, fares

### Departure tax — **CHANGED, and it affects you**

**Now ¥3,000 per departure**, up from ¥1,000, **effective for departures on/after 1 July 2026** ([mailmate](https://mailmate.jp/blog/japan-departure-tax), [shiho-tax](https://www.shiho-tax.com/international-tourist-tax/), [Nikkei](https://www.nikkei.com/article/DGXZQOUA119NT0R11C25A2000000/)).

**Transitional relief:** tickets issued or contracted **before 1 July 2026** keep the ¥1,000 rate even for a later departure. So if you booked your November flights before 30 June, you're grandfathered. Collected inside the ticket price — nothing to pay at the airport.

### ⚠️ Tax-free shopping changes **mid-month, on 1 November 2026**

This is the sharpest planning trap in the whole brief. From **1 Nov 2026** Japan switches from exemption-at-the-register to **pay-then-refund-at-departure** ([japan-guide](https://www.japan-guide.com/news/tax-free-shopping.html), [JNTO](https://www.japan.travel/en/ca/news/changes-are-coming-to-tax-free-shopping-in-japan/)).

If your trip straddles 1 November, **purchases before that date use the old system** (10% simply deducted at checkout) and **purchases from 1 Nov use the new one** (you pay full 10% and reclaim at the airport). **Front-load significant shopping into late October if you can.**

New-system mechanics: ¥5,000 pre-tax per store per day minimum (unchanged); the ¥500,000 consumables cap is **abolished**; the general-goods/consumables split and sealed-packaging rule are **abolished**; a single 90-day export window; claim at a customs kiosk or via Visit Japan Web **before check-in**. ⚠️ *Refund method (cash/card/app) and whether a handling fee applies are not specified in official material.*

1. **The trip has an unavoidable internal conflict.** Shosoin (ends 9 Nov) and the tax-free system change (1 Nov) pull early; peak foliage in Kyoto/Nara/Tokyo pulls to Nov 20–Dec 2. You cannot have both. Hakone is the one destination that works either way.
2. **Avoid Kyoto on 21–23 November** — a three-day weekend landing on peak foliage is the worst crowd scenario of the month.
3. **Skip the JR Pass**, use Smart EX, and take the ¥580 local train Kyoto→Osaka.
4. **Front-load big shopping before 1 November** to keep register-side tax exemption.
5. **Two events on the brief are dead:** the Gaien Ginkgo Festival (not held since 2019) and Arashiyama Hanatouro (ended 2021). **Kobe Luminarie is now a late-January event.** Jidai Matsuri is October.
6. **Recheck in September** for: 2026 koyo forecasts, all Kyoto illumination dates, the Gaien light-up window, Nara deer antler cutting, and the Hakone Daimyo Gyoretsu official posting. **Recheck late August** for Shosoin tickets.

Suica / PASMO / ICOCA are mutually interoperable nationwide and work for trains, buses, konbini, vending machines, and many lockers — **this is the single most useful payment instrument to have.** Load them via Apple Wallet if possible, which sidesteps the physical-card supply issues. Japanese card terminals and Seven Bank ATMs will frequently offer to charge you **"in USD"** rather than yen. **Always decline and choose JPY.** DCC embeds a 3–7% markup on top of whatever your card already charges. **None. Anywhere.** Not restaurants, not taxis, not hotels, not guides. Attempting to tip creates awkwardness and staff may chase you down to return the money. # 10-Day Japan Itinerary Draft — November 2026, 2 people, first time

**Structure note first (important):** Tokyo 4 + Hakone 1 + Kyoto 3 + Osaka 2 = **10 nights, i.e. 11 calendar days on the ground**. Below is built as Day 1–Day 11 (Day 11 = departure). Also note Kyoto's "3 nights" yields only ~2 full days — I've solved that by making **Nara the transfer day between Kyoto and Osaka** rather than a round-trip from Osaka, which frees a genuine full Osaka day.

---

## 1. NOVEMBER SPECIFICS

### Autumn foliage (koyo) — and the "running late" caveat

Textbook peak windows ([japan-guide](https://www.japan-guide.com/e/e2014_when.html)):

| Place | Typical peak |
|---|---|
| Tokyo | Late Nov – early Dec |
| Hakone | Mid – late Nov |
| Kyoto | Mid – late Nov |
| Nara | Late Nov – early Dec |

**The caveat is real and large.** Actual observed peaks in recent years ran markedly late:
- **2024:** Tokyo peak reported **Dec 3**, Kyoto peak **Dec 4** — roughly 1–2 weeks past the textbook window. Reports cited "temperatures far above average over the past weeks and months, discouraging trees from starting their coloring process." ([koyo24 report](https://www.japan-guide.com/blog/koyo24/))
- **2025:** Kyoto peak began ~**Nov 22** and was "still in full swing" on **Nov 29**; Tokyo peaked ~**Nov 26**. ([koyo25 report](https://www.japan-guide.com/blog/koyo25/))

**Planning implication:** for foliage, weight your trip *late*. A trip ending in early December beats one ending Nov 20. Do not book mid-November expecting peak Kyoto color.

**Hakone is the exception — elevation makes it earlier.** Owakudani/Sengokuhara (~1,000m+) turn first, typically late Oct–early Nov; Lake Ashi mid-Nov; Hakone-Yumoto (lowest) late Nov. So in mid-to-late November you'll likely catch *upper* Hakone already past peak and the *lower* valley at its best — the ropeway ride may be bare while Yumoto is glowing.

### Weather and packing

November is one of Japan's most reliable months — dry, clear, low typhoon risk. Broadly: Tokyo/Kyoto/Osaka/Nara highs ~17°C early month falling to ~12°C late month; lows ~10°C falling to ~5°C. **Hakone runs 5–8°C colder** than Tokyo and is genuinely cold at night at Owakudani elevation.

Pack: layers (t-shirt + midlayer + light insulated or shell jacket), one warm layer for Hakone, a compact umbrella, **comfortable broken-in walking shoes** (you will do 15–20k steps/day), and **slip-on-friendly shoes** — you'll remove them constantly at temples and ryokan. Early vs late November is roughly one layer's difference. Indoor heating is aggressive, so avoid bulky single-piece coats.

*Flag: I could not re-verify station-by-station JMA climate normals within budget; treat the temperature figures as standard published averages rather than freshly confirmed.*

### Public holidays — November 2026

Verified against the Cabinet Office official holiday list ([www8.cao.go.jp](https://www8.cao.go.jp/chosei/shukujitsu/gaiyou.html)):

- **Culture Day (文化の日) — Tuesday, November 3, 2026**
- **Labour Thanksgiving Day (勤労感謝の日) — Monday, November 23, 2026**
- **No substitute holidays (振替休日) in November 2026** — neither date falls on a Sunday.

**What this means for you:**
- **Nov 23 is a Monday → Sat 21 / Sun 22 / Mon 23 is a three-day weekend**, and it lands squarely on likely-near-peak Kyoto foliage. This is the single worst crowding window of the month. Kyoto's Higashiyama, Arashiyama and Tofuku-ji will be genuinely unpleasant. Shinkansen reserved seats sell out. **Avoid being in Kyoto Nov 21–23, and avoid travelling by Shinkansen on Nov 23.**
- **Nov 3 (Tue, Culture Day):** museums are busy; **Tsukiji Outer Market is closed** (it closes Sundays *and national holidays*); the Hakone Daimyo Gyoretsu procession traditionally runs this date in Hakone-Yumoto with road closures.
- General rule: **every November weekend** at Kyoto foliage sites is heavy. Weekday mornings are transformatively better.

### November events

- **Shosoin Exhibition, Nara National Museum — CONFIRMED for 2026: Oct 24 – Nov 9, 2026**, open every day during the run, 8:00–18:00 (Fri/Sat/Sun/holidays until 20:00), last entry 60 min before close. This is the once-a-year airing of the 8th-century Shosoin treasures and it is a major crowd generator in Nara. **Admission price was still unannounced as of my check — the site states ticket info will be published "late August."** ([shosoin-ten.jp](https://shosoin-ten.jp/), [narahaku.go.jp](https://www.narahaku.go.jp/news/20260714_15715/))
- **Tokyo illuminations** (2025 dates as proxy; 2026 not yet announced): Rikugien **Nov 28–Dec 9**, ¥1,200 (¥1,000 online), 18:00–20:30; Jingu Gaien Ginkgo Avenue **Nov 22–30**, 16:30–19:30; Showa Memorial Park **Oct 30–Nov 30**, 16:30–21:00. ([japan-guide Tokyo autumn](https://www.japan-guide.com/e/e3061.html))
- **Hakone Daimyo Gyoretsu** — traditionally November 3. *Flag: I could not confirm the 2026 edition on the Hakone Tourist Association site.*
- *Flag — could not confirm within budget:* Tori-no-ichi 2026 dates (they fall on "Rooster days," typically 2–3 dates in November), Arashiyama Momiji Festival, Kobe Luminarie 2026. Note Arashiyama **Hanatouro was discontinued** (2021) — do not plan around it; I did not re-verify this.

- **Tokyo National Museum: closed Mondays.** ¥1,000, 9:30–17:00 (Fri/Sat to 20:00). Note: **suitcases are no longer allowed inside.**

- **Meiji Jingu Museum: closed Thursdays.**

## 3. HAKONE

### Ropeway status — VERIFIED OPERATING

**The full Hakone Ropeway line (Sounzan – Owakudani – Togendai) is currently running with no suspended sections.** Hours **9:00–17:00 (Feb–Nov)**. The operator continuously monitors volcanic gas concentration and displays it live; suspensions are decided on multiple gas readings and are **not** tied to the eruption alert level. ([hakonenavi.jp/hakone-ropeway](https://www.hakonenavi.jp/hakone-ropeway/)) Fares were revised as of Oct 1, 2025. The only current disruption notice on the official English site concerns the **Hakone Kyukaido bus line**, not the ropeway. ([hakonenavi English](https://www.hakonenavi.jp/international/en/))

**But there IS a restriction you should know:** Owakudani remains a designated 警戒区域 (alert zone). The **Owakudani Nature Research Path (自然研究路)** — closed since 2015 — has reopened only on **guided entry requiring advance online reservation plus an ¥800 cooperation fee**. A ~3km hiking route through Komagatake/Owakudani is still closed, and the prefectural road to the parking area is open only 09:00–17:00. Kanagawa Prefecture warns that volcanic gas is present and that people with respiratory or cardiac conditions should avoid the area. ([pref.kanagawa.jp](https://www.pref.kanagawa.jp/docs/j8g/cnt/f532566/), updated 2026-05-27) **The ordinary Owakudani ropeway station area — including the black-egg shops — does not require this reservation.** Only the research path does.

### The loop, in order

Hakone-Yumoto → **Tozan Railway** (switchbacks) → Gora → **Cablecar** → Sounzan → **Ropeway** → Owakudani (get off) → Togendai → **Lake Ashi pirate ship** → Moto-Hakone / Hakone-machi → **Tozan Bus** back to Hakone-Yumoto. ([japan-guide Hakone](https://www.japan-guide.com/e/e5200.html))

Approximate leg times (standard published figures, not individually re-verified): Yumoto→Gora ~40 min; Gora→Sounzan ~10 min; Sounzan→Togendai ~30 min through-riding plus your Owakudani stop; boat ~30–40 min; bus back to Yumoto ~40 min. **Budget 5–6 hours for the full circuit with stops** — not 3.

**Do the ropeway and lake in the MORNING**, for Fuji.

### Costs

- **Hakone Free Pass: ¥7,100 from Shinjuku (2-day), ¥6,000 from Odawara (2-day).** Covers the entire loop — Tozan railway, cablecar, ropeway, pirate ship, Tozan buses — plus the Odakyu line to Hakone. **Romancecar limited express is a separate ¥1,200 surcharge each way** (~¥1,150 as an e-ticket). Round trip Shinjuku with Romancecar both ways ≈ ¥9,500. Buy it; it pays for itself on the loop alone. *Flag: I saw no 3-day variant confirmed.*
- **Hakone Open-Air Museum: ¥2,000 adult (¥1,800 buying online), 9:00–17:00 (last entry 16:30), open year-round with no closing days.** ([hakone-oam.or.jp](https://www.hakone-oam.or.jp/en/)) Allow 1.5–2 hours. It's genuinely excellent and works even in poor weather.
- **Lake Ashi cruise:** covered by the Free Pass. *Flag: standalone fare and Special Cabin surcharge not confirmed.*
- **Owakudani black eggs (kuro-tamago):** sold at the station shop. *Flag: current price not confirmed.*

### Hakone Shrine torii ("Heiwa no Torii")

Free, on the lakeshore a short walk from Moto-Hakone port. **There is now a photo queue** — typically 20 minutes to over an hour in peak season and afternoons, with an understood ~3-minute-per-party limit. Arriving before 08:00 cuts the wait to ~15 minutes. There is no formally published restriction policy, so treat the 3-minute limit as etiquette, not law. Reports indicate the gate underwent temporary repair work in early 2026 but has reopened — **worth re-checking before you go.**

### Mt Fuji odds

November is one of the **best** months: cold, dry air gives high visibility, and November–February morning visibility from north-side viewpoints runs very high (vs ~27% in June). **Morning, roughly 06:00–08:00, is dramatically better than afternoon** — cloud builds through the day. Best Hakone vantages: the ropeway between Owakudani and Togendai, and the lake from the boat looking north. Check [isfujivisible.com](https://isfujivisible.com/) the night before and, if it forecasts clear, get on the first cablecar.

### Ryokan and logistics

Book a ryokan in **Gora or Sengokuhara** with in-room or private onsen if either of you has tattoos — many public baths still refuse them, and a private bath removes the question entirely. Kaiseki dinner is typically served early (17:30–19:00) and is fixed at booking; **do not plan evening sightseeing.** Notify dietary restrictions at reservation, not on arrival.

**Luggage:** forward your main suitcases **Tokyo hotel → Kyoto hotel** by takkyubin on the morning of your Hakone departure. Roughly **¥3,200 per suitcase under 25kg, next-day delivery**; arrange at your hotel front desk. ([japan-guide](https://www.japan-guide.com/e/e2278.html)) Carry one overnight bag to Hakone. Coin lockers exist at Hakone-Yumoto but fill early on autumn weekends.

This is the part that determines whether Kyoto is magical or miserable.

## 1. Kiyomizu-dera & southern Higashiyama

**Kiyomizu-dera** — Adult **¥500**, students ¥200. Hours **6:00–18:00** (18:30 Jul–Aug). **No closing days.** Time needed 60–90 min.

Autumn night viewing (*yoru no tokubetsu haikan*): the temple's own gate-front association lists **2026: Nov 21–30, reception 17:30–21:00** (Jojuin garden 18:00–20:30) — [monzenkai.com/yakan](https://www.monzenkai.com/yakan). **2025 actual was Nov 22–Dec 7**, 17:30–21:30 (last entry 21:00), **¥500** adult ([kyoto-kanko-mapping](https://kyoto-kanko-mapping.com/autumn_leaves_lightup_map/), [souda-kyoto](https://souda-kyoto.jp/event/detail/lightup-autumn.html)). ⚠️ The 2026 window is listed as much shorter (10 days vs 16) — worth re-checking in September 2026. **Could not definitively confirm** whether a daytime ticket carries over; the standard practice is that the grounds clear at 18:00 and evening entry is a **separate ¥500**. Budget for paying twice.

**Sannenzaka / Ninenzaka** — Free, always open. Dead before 08:00, solid wall of people 10:00–16:00. Tripods and selfie sticks are discouraged; no formal fine here.

**Yasaka Pagoda (Hokan-ji)** — Interior **¥400** (junior-high age and up only; under-13s not admitted, steep stairs). Roughly **10:00–15:00/16:00 but opening days are irregular** — often shut; phone 075-551-2417. Treat entry as a bonus. The classic photo is from Yasaka-dori looking up, best before 08:00.

**Kodai-ji** — Official site: adult **¥800**, JHS/HS ¥400; **combined with Entoku-in ¥1,200**; 9:00–17:30 (recept. 17:00) ([kodaiji.com/haikan.html](https://www.kodaiji.com/haikan.html)). ⚠️ japan-guide still shows the older ¥600 / ¥900-combo figures — the official ¥800 is the one to trust. Autumn illumination **2025: Oct 24–Dec 14, 17:00–22:00 (recept. 21:30), ¥600**; Entoku-in same dates, ¥500. 2026 dates not yet posted. Kodai-ji has the **longest** autumn light-up window in Kyoto — very useful insurance against a late peak.

**Yasaka Shrine** — Free, always open, no closing days, 10–20 min. **Maruyama Park** — free, 24h; pleasant but it's a cherry-blossom park, not a top autumn site.

**Gion / Hanamikoji** — Photography is **banned on the private alleys** (not on Hanamikoji itself or other public streets), with signage threatening a **¥10,000 fine**, introduced Oct 2019 by the local *machizukuri* council. Enforcement is by residents/local council rather than police, and the fine is a private penalty of contested legal force — but signage and confrontation are real, and enforcement steps up in peak season. Practical rule: **stay on Hanamikoji and marked public roads, never photograph geiko/maiko without consent, never follow them.** Shirakawa canal area is quieter and less restricted. ## 2. Fushimi Inari Taisha

**Free, open 24h, no closing days** ([japan-guide](https://www.japan-guide.com/e/e3915.html)). ## 7. Autumn leaves — timing and ranking

**Typical Kyoto city peak: ~Nov 20 – Dec 5.** But recent years have run **late**:

- **2023** peak reported **Nov 26**
- **2024** peak reported **Dec 4** — described in Japanese sources as the latest in eight years, caused by high temperatures through mid-November
- **2025** peak reported **Nov 29**, with pre-season forecasts again calling for "later than average" after a very warm September/October

([japan-guide autumn color report archive](https://www.japan-guide.com/e/e2014.html), [blog.kanko.jp](https://blog.kanko.jp/))

## 9. Crowd-avoidance summary

- **Fushimi Inari:** through the gate by **06:45–07:00**, or after 20:00. Peak 10:00–16:00.
- **Kiyomizu-dera:** **06:00–07:30** (it opens at 06:00 — almost uniquely early, and this is Kyoto's single best crowd hack). Or return for the 17:30 night opening. Avoid 10:00–16:00.
- **Arashiyama bamboo grove:** **before 08:00**, ideally 07:00–07:30. By 09:30 it's shoulder-to-shoulder. Pair with Tenryu-ji's **07:30 autumn opening (Nov 14–30, 2026)**.
- **Tofuku-ji:** in the queue before the **08:30** autumn opening.
- **Nishiki Market:** 10:00–11:00.
- Kyoto's crowds are strongly weekday-dependent in November: **avoid weekends entirely** if your three days allow it, and note that the Nov 23 Labour Thanksgiving holiday creates a long weekend most years.

## 10. Kyoto transit

**The bus-only one-day pass is DISCONTINUED** — sales ended **30 September 2023** (it was ¥700), explicitly to reduce tourist crowding on city buses ([city.kyoto.lg.jp/kotsu/page/0000309762.html](https://www.city.kyoto.lg.jp/kotsu/page/0000309762.html)).

Current options:
- **Subway & Bus One-Day Pass: ¥1,100 adult / ¥550 child.** Covers all subway lines, all city buses, Kyoto Bus, Keihan Bus and West JR Bus (some routes excluded). This is the pass to buy — but only if you'll make 5+ rides.
- **Subway One-Day Pass: ¥800.**
- **City bus flat fare: ¥230** in the central zone.

**The bus overcrowding problem is real** — buses on the Kiyomizu/Ginkaku-ji corridors regularly pass stops full, and luggage is discouraged. Kyoto's answer is the **Sightseeing Limited Express Bus**:
- **EX100** — Kyoto Station → Kiyomizu-dera (Gojozaka) → Gion → Heian Shrine → Ginkaku-ji
- **EX101** — Kyoto Station → Kiyomizu-dera only (short shuttle)
- **Kyoto Station to Kiyomizu-dera in 10 minutes**, vs 20+ on the local 206
- **Fare ¥500 adult / ¥250 child cash** — more than double the normal bus fare, but **the ¥1,100 Subway & Bus One-Day Pass IS valid** on it
- **Board at the front, pay on boarding**, exit at the rear (opposite of normal Kyoto buses)
- EX100 runs roughly **every 7–8 minutes in the morning**; both depart Kyoto Station bus terminal **stop D1**
- Verdict: **worth it.** ([city.kyoto.lg.jp/kotsu/webguide/ja/bus/limited_express.html](https://www2.city.kyoto.lg.jp/kotsu/webguide/ja/bus/limited_express.html))

**IC cards:** ICOCA/Suica/PASMO and the rest of the ten-card family work on **virtually all trains and buses in and around Kyoto**, including city buses and the subway. Buy or top up ICOCA at any JR West machine including Kyoto Station. Mobile Suica/ICOCA on iPhone works for foreign visitors (Apple Wallet, no Japanese card needed for Suica); Welcome Suica is a Tokyo-airport product and unnecessary here. ⚠️ The news about dropping IC cards concerns **rural** operators (Kumamoto, parts of Kyushu/Shikoku), **not Kansai** — Kyoto is unaffected.

**Taxis:** base **¥500 for the first 0.9 km**, then ¥100 per 255 m; 20% surcharge 22:00–05:00. **Kyoto Station → Kiyomizu-dera ≈ ¥1,410** — for two or more people that beats the bus on both cost and time, and this is the single best money-for-sanity trade in Kyoto. Use the **GO** app (Uber in Kyoto mostly dispatches the same taxi fleet). Expect scarcity at 17:00–19:00 in late November and after night illuminations end — walk a few blocks to a main road rather than waiting outside a temple gate.

**Rail alternatives to buses:** the two subway lines (Karasuma N–S, Tozai E–W) miss most temples, so use **Keihan** (Fushimi Inari via JR, but Gion-Shijo / Kiyomizu-Gojo / Tofukuji for Higashiyama), **Hankyu** (Kyoto-Kawaramachi for downtown/Gion), **JR Sagano Line** (Kyoto → Saga-Arashiyama, 15 min) and the **Randen tram** (Arashiyama ↔ Kinkaku-ji area via Kitano-Hakubaicho). Bicycle rental (¥1,000–1,500/day) is genuinely efficient in flat central Kyoto but poor for Arashiyama/Fushimi.

| **Nara** | 16.5 °C | 6.4 °C | 71 mm | ~8 |

Sources: [Tokyo](https://weather-and-climate.com/Tokyo-November-averages), [Kyoto](https://weather-and-climate.com/kyoto-November-averages), [Osaka](https://weather-and-climate.com/osaka-November-averages), [Hakone](https://weather-and-climate.com/hakone-November-averages), [Nara](https://www.weather-atlas.com/en/japan/nara-weather-november). These are aggregator figures, broadly consistent with JMA 1991–2020 normals; I could not pull the JMA English normals table cleanly, so treat them as ±1 °C.

**Early vs late November is a real difference, not a rounding error.** Kyoto drops from ~20 °C at the start of the month to ~14 °C by the end; Nara from ~19 °C to ~14 °C. Early November is light-jacket weather; late November mornings and evenings are genuinely cold, especially inland Kyoto/Nara where the overnight low sits near 5 °C.

Three things that break naive packing:

1. **Diurnal swing, not absolute cold.** Kyoto's 17/7 °C spread means a 10 °C change within a day. Kyoto and Nara are basins — they trap cold air overnight and the mornings bite far more than "average high 17 °C" suggests.
2. **Hakone is a different climate zone.** The 17.5/7.1 °C figure is the town average; Sengokuhara and Gora run 3–4 °C colder, and Owakudani at ~1,000 m is colder again and windy on the ropeway. Bring a proper insulating layer for the Hakone day even if Tokyo is mild.
3. **Evening illuminations are the coldest thing you'll do.** Kyoto temple light-ups and the Gaien ginkgo light-up run to 19:30–21:00, standing still, in late November. This is where people are underdressed.

**Pack:** merino/synthetic base layers; a mid-layer fleece or light down (packable down is ideal — it handles Owakudani and stuffs into a daypack the rest of the time); a **water-resistant** shell rather than a wool coat (Kyoto averages ~16 rainy days in November — the wettest of the five by frequency, though the totals are modest, so it's drizzle rather than downpours); a compact umbrella (universally used in Japan, cheap at any konbini if you'd rather buy on arrival); **comfortable waterproof-ish walking shoes** — Kyoto/Nara temple days run 15–20 k steps on gravel and stone; and **easily removable shoes** since you'll be in and out of temples constantly — loafers or zip boots beat laces. Add a light scarf and gloves if you're travelling late November. Onsen ryokan supply yukata and towels, so don't pack sleepwear for Hakone.

## 3. Public holidays and crowding

**Confirmed against the Japanese Cabinet Office** ([cao.go.jp](https://www8.cao.go.jp/chosei/shukujitsu/gaiyou.html)) and [publicholidays.jp](https://publicholidays.jp/2026-dates/):

| Holiday | Date | Day |
|---|---|---|
| **Culture Day (文化の日)** | **3 November 2026** | **Tuesday** |
| **Labour Thanksgiving Day (勤労感謝の日)** | **23 November 2026** | **Monday** |

**No substitute holiday (振替休日) applies in November 2026.** Substitute holidays only trigger when a holiday falls on a Sunday; neither does. (2026 does have substitute/bridge days, but they fall on **6 May** and **22 September** — not November.)

November 2026 weekends: **Nov 7–8, 14–15, 21–22, 28–29.** Nov 1 is a Sunday.

### What this means in practice

- **Mon 2 Nov is a bridge day.** With Culture Day on a Tuesday, large numbers of Japanese workers take Monday 2 Nov off to make Sat 31 Oct – Tue 3 Nov a four-day break. **Treat Oct 31 – Nov 3 as a domestic travel peak.** Hakone, Nikko and Kyoto hotels will be expensive and full; book well ahead.
- **Sat 21 – Mon 23 Nov is a true three-day weekend** (Labour Thanksgiving on a Monday). This is the single worst period of the entire trip window, because **it collides almost exactly with peak Kyoto foliage.** If your dates are flexible at all, avoid Kyoto on 21–23 November. If they aren't, do Kyoto's marquee sites at dawn and save the three-day weekend for something lower-profile.
- **Sat 7 Nov** is a double-hit in Tokyo: Ichi-no-tori (§4) falls on a Saturday, which is unusual and drives much heavier crowds than a weekday fair.
- **Sun 15 Nov is Shichi-Go-San** — major congestion at Meiji Jingu, Hie Shrine, Tomioka Hachimangu and the surrounding weekends, plus lots of families in formal dress (charming, but slow-moving).
- **Tue 3 Nov (Culture Day)** in Hakone means the Daimyo Gyoretsu procession closes Route 1 through Hakone-Yumoto roughly 11:00–15:00. Do not plan to move around Hakone by car or bus that afternoon.

### Kyoto weekend crowding generally

The **last two weeks of November are among the most crowded periods in Kyoto's entire year**, and weekends within the Nov 18–30 window are severely congested at the headline sites. Specific mitigations that actually work:

- **Weekday mornings before 10:00.** On weekends and holidays, make it **08:00**.
- **Kiyomizudera opens at 06:00** — arriving at opening is the single highest-leverage move in Kyoto.
- **Tofukuji** is the worst offender: large crowds form immediately at opening, and the Tsutenkyo Bridge becomes a no-stopping shuffle. japan-guide's 21 Nov 2025 report flagged it explicitly. There is a reservation-only early-morning private viewing worth investigating.
- **Philosopher's Path after 16:00** is pleasant when the day-trippers have gone.
- Kyoto City is actively pushing six peripheral districts — **Fushimi, Ohara, Takao, Yamashina, Nishikyo, Keihoku** — to decompress the centre. Ohara and Takao also peak *earlier* (mid-Nov), so they solve a timing problem and a crowd problem at once.

## 5. Money: taxes, JR Pass, fares

### Departure tax — **CHANGED, and it affects you**

**Now ¥3,000 per departure**, up from ¥1,000, **effective for departures on/after 1 July 2026** ([mailmate](https://mailmate.jp/blog/japan-departure-tax), [shiho-tax](https://www.shiho-tax.com/international-tourist-tax/), [Nikkei](https://www.nikkei.com/article/DGXZQOUA119NT0R11C25A2000000/)).

**Transitional relief:** tickets issued or contracted **before 1 July 2026** keep the ¥1,000 rate even for a later departure. So if you booked your November flights before 30 June, you're grandfathered. Collected inside the ticket price — nothing to pay at the airport.

### ⚠️ Tax-free shopping changes **mid-month, on 1 November 2026**

This is the sharpest planning trap in the whole brief. From **1 Nov 2026** Japan switches from exemption-at-the-register to **pay-then-refund-at-departure** ([japan-guide](https://www.japan-guide.com/news/tax-free-shopping.html), [JNTO](https://www.japan.travel/en/ca/news/changes-are-coming-to-tax-free-shopping-in-japan/)).

If your trip straddles 1 November, **purchases before that date use the old system** (10% simply deducted at checkout) and **purchases from 1 Nov use the new one** (you pay full 10% and reclaim at the airport). **Front-load significant shopping into late October if you can.**

New-system mechanics: ¥5,000 pre-tax per store per day minimum (unchanged); the ¥500,000 consumables cap is **abolished**; the general-goods/consumables split and sealed-packaging rule are **abolished**; a single 90-day export window; claim at a customs kiosk or via Visit Japan Web **before check-in**. ⚠️ *Refund method (cash/card/app) and whether a handling fee applies are not specified in official material.*

## Planning implications

1. **The trip has an unavoidable internal conflict.** Shosoin (ends 9 Nov) and the tax-free system change (1 Nov) pull early; peak foliage in Kyoto/Nara/Tokyo pulls to Nov 20–Dec 2. You cannot have both. Hakone is the one destination that works either way.
2. **Avoid Kyoto on 21–23 November** — a three-day weekend landing on peak foliage is the worst crowd scenario of the month.
3. **Skip the JR Pass**, use Smart EX, and take the ¥580 local train Kyoto→Osaka.
4. **Front-load big shopping before 1 November** to keep register-side tax exemption.
